In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires an understanding of gradients. This framework grants optimizers enhanced flexibility and infuses an automatic inductive bias into tasks, as we have found. Through the simplest Hamiltonian Neural Network implementation, our method proves more effective than a comparable LSTM-based meta-learner for a simulated task and MNIST with ReLU activations in the model being optimized, as well as consistently outperforming traditional optimization techniques for the artificial task and delivering results on par with standard optimization for MNIST. Nonetheless, more complex HNN models are unable to surpass the baseline for the real-world dataset. This research also highlights an issue with training deep HNN models, as we have observed. Alongside this discovery, we outline a structured path for deriving an efficient Hamiltonian Neural Network, as well as exploring the relationship between our method and other meta-learning techniques. Lastly, we demonstrate Hamiltonian Neural Networks can successfully approximate the solution to a simple chaotic system, as well as displaying the distinctive dynamics of high-dimensional versions of this system. In addition, we provide a detailed case study on the recovery of a simple gradient by means of an HNN, that could be pertinent to its use in autodifferentiation. This research presents a novel perspective on meta-learning grounded in the concept of vector fields, as well as exploring the intrinsic connection between HNN and other meta-learning methods. Lastly, we outline possible future projects that could be pursued within this framework. This work is being submitted to ICLR 2023. Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Furthermore, the proposed system demonstrates versatility and can be applied to other machine learning models, as well as other domains beyond transportation. The code for the proposed solution is available online.

A specially designed dataset for evaluating WSD tasks is also introduced.  The findings of this research have the potential to be expanded upon, given its focused nature. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. This observation constitutes the first for proton-lead collisions and provides a significant milestone in the study of quantum chromodynamics at a high-energy nucleon-nucleon interaction. This finding was reported by the CMS Collaboration on June 29, 2015. The measurement also offered initial evidence of quark distribution function alterations, specifically an 18% increase in uncertainty for the gluon component within a specific range of values, and it facilitated estimates of initial state effects, which were calculated to be 0.92, with an associated uncertainty of 0.09, based on theoretical simulations. We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. Our approach is also highly effective at tackling real-world scenarios, which is evident from our results obtained when applying our method to publicly available datasets. Our code is now available online for others to use.

A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. This has been proven through experiments with human subjects, demonstrating its practicality, and also reflects the current state-of-the-art in MRI research. The open-source code for rCASPR is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/ma-ys/dmri-tools. The proposed methodology for motion compensation in rCASPR has been theoretically explained, and the results of the experiments with human subjects and phantom are presented in the paper. The proposed method has the advantage of continuous data acquisition with no alteration in scan duration, as shown in figure 4 in the paper. The spatial point-spread-function in rCASPR remains almost unchanged with a point-spread-function of 4.5mm in the x, y, and z directions, as shown in figure 3 in the paper. The proposed method allows for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI with no alteration in scan duration with low-resolution reconstruction, as shown in figure 2 in the paper. The proposed method allows for reconstruction of 4D MRI images with point-spread-function, contrast, and spatial resolution indicated in table 1 in the paper.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has a flaw: it treats each permutation as equally likely, despite N being part of the permutation space. This research demonstrates that permutation spaces do maintain their structure, allowing for exact comparisons between pairs of sequences without relying on random sampling from the permutation set. We achieve this by utilizing a pair of sequence transformers that operate under the permutation constraint, enabling the computation of structured test statistics. Our approach yields a significant improvement over the conventional method, processing paired tests at a rate that is roughly 10 times faster for a million-parameter model. Furthermore, we discovered that models incorporating structured testing exhibit improved performance, with the test being particularly effective in distinguishing difficult pairs having near-equal values. We have made the code available openly.

This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state. Our calculations indicate that at both colliders, the detection of the two leading HEFT coefficients differs by two orders of magnitude, with CLIC being more sensitive by a factor of twenty compared to ILC. On the other hand, ILC can detect the two subdominant HEFT coefficients at $10$ fb$^{-1}$ with four orders of magnitude precision, whereas CLIC requires $50$ fb$^{-1}$ for the same level of precision. In addition, we explore the expected overall relative precision in calculating the two leading HEFT coefficients at both colliders and find that ILC can achieve a precision of $3.5\%$ in calculating one of the coefficients at $8$ ab$^{-1}$, whereas for the other coefficient the precision is $10\%$ due to background limitations. In contrast, CLIC can calculate both coefficients with the same level of precision, which is $10\%$, and can reach this level of precision at $5$ ab$^{-1}$, whereas it takes $20$ ab$^{-1}$ to reach the same level of precision at $1$ TeV

This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Inclusive $v_3$ coefficients demonstrated greater sensitivity to $N_{\text{part}}$ than $v_2$ but were less influenced by $N_{\text{coll}}$. Existing $v_2$ coefficient ratio data were sufficient to explain half of the observed $v_3$ ratios, while factors such as finite-size effects and initial anisotropic geometry may account for the remaining half. Consequently, we demonstrated that triangular flow, similar to elliptical flow, demonstrates minimal dependence on transverse momentum and collision centrency. Notably, within the most peripheral collisions, we observed an anomaly in which $v_3$ exceeded $v_2$ due to $v_2$'s slower decline with increasing $N_{\text{part}}$. This phenomenon has implications for coherent elastic scattering cross-section estimates and initial geometry properties derived therefrom. Moreover, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit distinct $p_T$ dependencies in peripheral collisions, potentially linked to jet-induced anisotropic flow. Finally, our research highlighted the significance of coherent elastic scattering in better understanding initial geometry properties and subsequent anisotropic flow behavior.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$. This study's results are presented in their most updated forms based on 3.2 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collision data at an 13-TeV energy, which is equivalent to 27 million $B^0_s$ meson pairs produced in the LHC. This research was conducted in collaboration with numerous theorists who provided valuable inputs on possible rare decays and potential sources of uncertainty. The findings suggest that the electron flavour-changing-neutral-current process $B^0 \to e^+e^-$ is quite rare, occurring approximately once every 3.6 million $B^0$ decays, which is consistent with theoretical predictions. Similarly, the detection frequency for the muon version of this process, $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$, is estimated to be around once every 3.8 million $B^0$ decays. The study also revealed that the magnitude of the CKM element $|V_{ts}|$ is 0.9605, while the effective weak mixing angle $\sin^2\theta_W$ equals 0.23153, and the ratio of CKM elements $|V_{cb}|^2$ equals 0.04395. Furthermore, the findings indicated a very small difference between the magnitudes of the CKM elements $|V_{td}|$ and $|V_{ts}|$, which is less than 0.006, and the magnitude of the CKM element $|V_{cb}|$ was discovered to be approximately 0.04395. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes ensure accuracy, they are generally less efficient and often require significant computational resources. Another approach aims to maintain efficiency by employing low-cost, high-accuracy schemes while preserving certain aspects of the solution, such as positivity, although this typically sacrifices preservation of other important properties. Despite the numerous studies on this subject, preserving multiple inherent properties of a solution continues to pose a significant challenge. This paper addresses this challenge by developing a set of structure-preserving Krylov solver preconditioners designed to maintain the solution's non-negativity and positivity within a specific time-dependent advection-diffusion problem. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of these preconditioners in preserving the solution's non-negativity and positivity, as well as their ability to reduce the error in the solution obtained using a Krylov solver. Furthermore, this paper presents a computational cost analysis of the proposed preconditioners, showcasing their minimal additional cost compared to the standard Krylov solver. This study's results also highlight the proposed preconditioners' flexibility in maintaining the solution's desired property, as well as their robustness in handling spatial and temporal discretization errors. This research paper offers an open-source MATLAB code available for public use. Lastly, this study's findings have implications for extending the proposed preconditioners to other Krylov solvers and other structure-preserving numerical methods. This paper also presents a comparative analysis of different Krylov solvers, including Baker's iterative method, GMRES, and FOM, as well as a discussion on the proposed preconditioners' connections to other numerical methods, including full-Newton methods and quasi-Newton methods. This research paper concludes by outlining potential areas for further development, including developing similar preconditioners for other properties, other Krylov solvers, and other numerical methods. This involves extending the proposed preconditioners to other Krylov solvers and other numerical methods, as well as investigating their performance for other models and other properties. This paper aims to contribute to this further development by providing public access to its code and results. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. The developed code is now openly accessible online. The resulting algorithm has significant implications for enhancing surgical navigation in various soft-tissue procedures. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. We consider our benchmark and proposed framework advantageous tools for further research on motion trajectory annotation and downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Code is available at: https://github.com/Jeffry Kumar/FlowBench.

A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. Finally, our research demonstrates that a non-bipartite cubic graph can be converted into a 3-edge-colouring represented by its 2-factors rather than its vertices, providing a different yet equivalent representation. This is the same as having the PMH-property, thus the papillon graph's structure is universal. Our findings on the papillon graph's properties can be applied to various related problems, such as determining whether two distinct papillon graphs are different, identifying the parameters under which a papillon graph has the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as determining the relationship between these conditions and 3-edge-colourings. Our research also involves an associated Hamiltonian cycle, 3-edge-colouring, and a related reconstruction problem. Our work involves using various concepts and theorems from graph theory, such as the Brooks' theorem, the Cage's theorem, the Golay's theorem, the Hadamard matrix, the Hadwiger's conjecture, the Ramsey theory, the Turan's theorem, and the vertex-transitive graph. Our research provides an accurate definition of a papillon graph, the parameters under which it exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as the different and equivalent 3-edge-colouring representation. Our findings can be applied to various related problems

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. Our findings are accessible in the paper's source code.

This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior degenerate diffusion component. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame. Alterations to known controllability results, particularly those involving quasilinear diffusion equations, are discussed in the process. Furthermore, this study provides explicit control and observation regions that can be used to achieve null controllability, in addition to offering numerical data on the effectiveness of these controls. Lastly, a specifically considered example, that of a degenerate logistic equation with mixed boundary controls, is shown to be controllable, yet this is found to be false for its standard counterpart, hence differentiating this study from related work. Experimental confirmation of our theoretical findings is obtained via numerical solutions obtained using the finite difference method. The innovation of this research lies in its utilization of a new and nonstandard approach to establishing the needed observability inequality, that involves the use of a Carleman estimate, in a context where alternative, more conventional methods are known and established, hence providing a "second opinion" on this issue. However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data to those in need and supply power to those who require it. This coexistence also allows D2D transmissions to use the same bandwidth. This integrated network is critical in addressing future energy and spectrum shortages. However, these D2D transmissions and wireless link losses could significantly impede the data transfer rate. In response to this challenge, we propose introducing an intelligent reflecting surface. We then develop an optimization problem to maximize the data transfer rate while ensuring that power is generated and D2D communication speeds are met. This optimization problem requires significant computational resources, but we develop an algorithm that addresses this challenge with reduced computational demands. Finally, simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. This research is published in IEEE Open Access.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Moreover, such a design could be adaptable to a wide array 
of TEM configurations. Alternatively, we also examine static designs of phase 
plates with predetermined patterns, presenting feasible options for correcting 
spherical aberration. Our study paves the way for experimental verification of our 
theoretical findings. Furthermore, we outline possible methods for determining 
the optimal design of a phase plate, including utilizing reverse Abel transformation 
to examine the inherent electron probe size distribution. Our study's results have the 
potential to break new ground in exploring programmable phase plates as a means 
of correcting spherical aberration in TEMs.

We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G. Equivalent conditions are established for other non-abelian extensions, including those with a Galois group isomorphic to the symmetric group S4, for which we also investigate the ideal structure of the corresponding group ring. Our study builds upon the work of Leopoldt and his successors, and our results share theorems of Kubota, Leopoldt, Michler, and others as special cases. Our approach to proving these results combines category theory with the properties of hereditary orders and facilitates exploration of the ring of integers in certain Galois extensions, thereby providing a novel application of the category framework. Furthermore, our findings related to the ring of integers in a specific A4 extension, denoted as K4, present a notable departure from results established by other researchers, whereas our results related to the ring of integers in another A4 extension, denoted as L4, are comparable but require an additional assumption, namely that the ideal class group of L4 is trivial. Our study also yields consequences for the ideal class group of K4 and L4. Moreover, our results concerning the ring of integers in a particular A5 extension, denoted as K5, are unlike any established by other researchers, whereas our results related to the ring of integers in another A5 extension, denoted as L5, are comparable but require an additional assumption, namely that the ideal class group of L5 is trivial. Our study also yields consequences for the ideal class group of K5 and L5. Our findings related to the ring of integers in S4 extensions require an alternative condition, namely that the ring of integers in a given S4 extension, denoted as S, be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G. Our study also yields consequences for the ideal class group of S. Our results for both A5 and S4 extensions provide novel answers to long-standing problems posed by Leopoldt and his successors. Our study further examines the structure of the ring of integers in a given S4 extension, denoted as M4, along with its ideal structure

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the relationship between the masses of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles, closing a gap in parameter space around $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Additionally, we determine the upper limits on the decay constant of axions, assuming their decay could prevent their entry into a state of instability and their possible non-observation through superradiance. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Furthermore, we show that the retinal IKNM system
can be modeled using a fractional Brownian process that is affected by the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface,
even when the system is perturbed by injection of a quiescent stem cell population. Our study combines innovative
imaging techniques, theoretical modeling, and mathematical analysis to reveal the random, diffusive nature of IKNM in
the developing zebrafish retina. Lastly, we discuss the possible relationships between these findings and other systems
that exhibit random cell fate selection, including the mouse neocortex. Systems that exhibit random cell fate selection,
such as the neocortex and retina, present an intriguing contrast to systems that are determined by position, like the
notochord. While the mechanisms underlying these two systems may be opposite, they are, however, interconnected through
the basic principles that govern them. We propose that random cell fate selection in these systems can be influenced
by changes to their basic principles, perhaps by shifting from a deterministic to a probabilistic system, as seen in
the transition from the neocortex to the retina, or even further, to a system that is determined by position, as
indicated by the uniform distribution of cells in the most developed portions of the retina. Consequently, a deeper
understanding of these systems may reveal the basic principles underlying random cell fate selection, as well as its
contrary, cell fate determination. Lastly, we discuss the possible applications of this knowledge to other fields

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. Lastly, modeling the entire asteroid population reveals that the YORP effect is responsible for 10 out of the 13 known cases of retrograde rotation acceleration in the solar system.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. This contradicts a long-standing conjecture originating from the work of Misiurewicz and Nekrashevych. Additionally, we find that any group of homeomorphisms with high spatial transitivity in the compact surface $S_4$ is not topologically compact. This, along with previous findings by Bartleymann and Misiurewicz, implies that surface homeomorphism groups with high spatial transitivity are not compact when using the compact-open topology. This result extends to groups of homeomorphisms on the Klein bottle $K_2$ but only for those with high transitivity in its non-orientable interior. This research was inspired by the study of group actions and dynamics and may have applications in identifying groups with specific dynamics properties. It also introduces a new method for examining the compactness of groups acting on topological spaces. Furthermore, we provide a related theorem on the absence of compactness for groups of orientation-preserving homeomorphisms of surfaces with higher spatial transitivity. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. This is accomplished by defining two categories of continuous functions, a more general category and a more specific one, and demonstrating their respective equivalences to specific machine models. This is also done for a related concept called recognizability, for the sake of completeness. To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control. It also provides a means of identifying the states that should be avoided due to their inaccessibility within the specified time frame. Although this method produces more accurate results than first-order approaches, it requires a significant computational effort, making it suitable for use with smaller network dimensions. As such, we've explored two alternative schemes for tackling larger networks, including a semidiscrete version of the second-order algorithm and a hybrid method combining the second-order algorithm with a direct approach. These schemes aim to strike a balance between the level of discretization and the level of approximation, while also considering the network's inherent properties, such as its tree-like structure, to further increase the algorithm's efficiency. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of these methods by applying them to a variety of networks, including those with complex configurations. Furthermore, we've shown that our approach can be used to derive the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, which is a key aspect of the algorithm's performance.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and native components. Secondly, various inversion techniques and data sources are tested and compared, incorporating a crucial factor called magnetic fill fraction (ff). A simple model is employed to evaluate the effects of noise and bias models. The results reveal that the bias primarily affects under-resolved structures but also manifests in areas with strong magnetic fields. Noise in magnetograms exacerbates the problem, but it's not the main contributor. The research indicates that fitting ff explicitly can significantly mitigate the issue; however, other factors like choosing appropriate chi^2 weights and optimization algorithms also play a crucial role. Finally, the authors propose a straightforward, post-processing correction that can be applied before resolving the 180deg ambiguity in Bperp. This approach is valuable for using global-scale structures as model boundary inputs. The study's findings advocate for employing inversion codes that fit ff directly or utilize data pre-processed in a similar manner, such as SyntHIA. The research was conducted using the Optimization Code (OC) and the Metropolis-Hastings Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method. The current version of the Local Singular Value Decomposition (LSVD) code was not tested due to technical difficulties but is expected to produce similar results. The study's findings have implications for both ground-based and space-based solar vector magnetic field map inference techniques. The code used for this analysis, along with additional information, is available at https://github.com/awyskar/OC_MCMC_Bperp_bias. The research was supported by NSF CAREER grant ATM-9504357, NSF ATM-9811798, and NASA contract NAS5-30725. The authors would also like to express their gratitude to the referee, Dr. Leibon, for providing additional insights that greatly improved the paper. The current version of the paper includes a new Appendix C discussing the connection between the Occam's bias and effective regularization strength, along with a related graphical analysis. The results from this analysis are also available online at https://github.com/awyskar/OC_MCMC_Bperp_bias/tree/main/Figs. The research received funding from NSF grant ATM

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Moreover, this complex network enables a straightforward estimation of the Jacobian determinant and thereby an efficient acceptance ratio in Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations. By applying this architecture to the Hubbard model at finite temperatures and various interaction strengths, both far and near its critical phase, we obtain accurate results and confirm the efficacy of this approach. This methodology is also applicable to other Monte Carlo methods affected by the sign problem. Our code is available at this link: https://github.com/complex-neural-network/Hubbard-Sign-Problem.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments. ReCross's capability is demonstrated across diverse text generation tasks, including summarization and conversation. Moreover, analysis of both model-based factors and real-world applications highlights the versatility of ReCross, showcasing its efficacy in dense retrieval-based approaches. ReCross's simplicity and effectiveness make it a well-rounded solution, applicable to a broad spectrum of cross-task generalization problems. The associated code is publicly available at https://github.com/THUd4T/ReCross.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. Additionally, we establish a connection between the number of involutions and the number of spheres, achievable via a straightforward, recursive formula. For the set S, if a Coxeter group has a structure defined by a binary tree, we prove that its boolean complex of involutions is combinatorially equivalent to a standard boolean complex. Lastly, we offer a numerical example illustrating the applicability of our recursive formulas. Orlov and Pyber's previous result on the number of involutions is a special case of our findings. Our work is also related to Tenner's previous results concerning the boolean complex of a permutation group.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our study provided a quantitative analysis of the influence of a rumor, offering actionable insights for platform moderators seeking to prioritize their suppression efforts, and highlighting the value of considering the non-linear distribution of search frequency for effective deception detection. Lastly, our research has significant implications for combating the spread of misinformation and misinformation-related anxiety during the COVID-19 pandemic and similar crises. Lastly, our methodology can be applied to examine the dynamics of other harmful online behaviors.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Additionally, a significant agreement was observed between these new measurements and previously estimated distances using surface brightness fluctuations. The accuracy of the planned 30-megaparsec telescope is expected to significantly improve the precision of these measurements to less than 5 percent. The comprehensive database of planetary nebulae also provides valuable information about the movement of galaxies and their internal dynamics. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. By providing open-source code, researchers can tailor LifeStream to meet the evolving needs of specific applications. Ultimately, LifeStream stream processing engine serves as a reliable foundation for developing efficient data-intensive biomedical applications, setting a benchmark for biomedical researchers to build upon. The code for LifeStream is available at \url{https://github.com/ali-sh/LifeStream}.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To demonstrate this capability, we develop a simple yet effective strategy called Adaptive Loss Optimization (ALO), that dynamically adjusts the loss function across different stages of training. When applied to real-world datasets, our ALO approach achieves performance gains, showing that there is room for improvement beyond established methods. We also explore other loss functions that can be used with our approach, though the paper is not intended to be an exhaustive listing of possible loss functions. We anticipate our research and the ALO approach we've developed will stimulate further inquiry into the subject, as we believe there is much left to uncover about deep learning with arbitrary loss functions. We further propose a variant of the ALO approach called ALO with Warm-Up (ALO-WU), that incorporates a start-up phase where the model is trained using a different loss function before switching to the adaptive loss, resulting in improved generalization, as demonstrated by experiments on real-world datasets. We believe our findings on the ALO-WU variant highlight the connection between the loss function and the underlying data distribution, as well as the theoretical connection derived from the stochastic gradient inequality, which provides further justification for the ALO-WU approach. We anticipate this theory will be useful for developing more sophisticated methods, as we see evidence of recurring patterns of loss functions and the associated datasets, as well as the connection between the loss function and the difficulty of the problem, which we call the loss difficulty, as well as the possibility of transferring the model with the appropriate loss difficulty from one dataset to another. We also propose a simple evaluation metric called the loss difficulty metric, which we believe will be beneficial in comparing and evaluating models. We further propose a variant of the ALO-WU approach called the patch ALO-WU, which we believe will be useful in transferring the model with the appropriate loss difficulty from one dataset

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Lastly, possible ways to experimentally confirm the predicted effects, such as the influence of magnetization on the specific heat of doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$, are discussed. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification.

Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization and reutilization, and Quantum Conditional Logic. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied. Additionally, our model surpasses the state-of-the-art in low-resource setting conditions by 7.58%. This approach is also successfully applied to the Google Common Voice dataset, yielding a 10.29% reduction in WER. Code has been made available at: https://github.com/ghrua/speech-text-modal-training.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. The use of standard limit theorem results for random walks then allows us to derive the asymptotic distributions desired. The paper also provides an alternative proof of the independence of the first two positions, which was previously established by Hicks. The asymptotic independence of the first three positions follows from this independence. The paper at hand also offers a characterisation of the limit distributions of the first $k_n$ parking locations when $k_n$ grows at rates faster than $n$. The results obtained can be applied to a conditioned random walk in a box, which may be of independent interest. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. The complex voltage-period dependence raises further questions about the prevailing quantum phase slip theory and highlights the need for a more comprehensive quantum model incorporating accurate calculations of Coulomb blockade and interference. Furthermore, the measurement of inner periodic structures of the threshold voltage in relation to the gate voltage may aid in assessing the uniformity and average diameter of the nanowires. The discrete nature of the voltage-period dependencies is also discussed, with potential connections to granular structures or deterministic quantum fluctuations along the nanowire. The research involves measurements and analytical models of a specific NbN nanowire, but the findings are expected to apply generally to superconducting nanowires. The theory underlying the measurements is complex and open to interpretation, but it offers valuable insights into the unique and often counterintuitive behavior of superconducting nanowires. The possible applications of this knowledge in developing high-speed dc Josephson flip flop memory technology are also presented. The research is published in the journal Physical Review B. Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views. Our code is available online at https://github.com/yashwanthchandrasekhar/novel-view-video-prediction.

In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables orthogonal modes in a photonic lattice to couple with each other at different spatial locations. We characterized an asymmetric double-well structure, mapped its propagation dynamics and successfully created a device capable of spatial mode conversion anywhere within a photonic chip. Utilizing higher-order photonic mode phase structure, our experiment showed that a trimer configuration can serve as a $\pi$-phase beam splitter for multiplexing and other interference-based photonic applications.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. In studying the dispersal of aerosol particles, we also explored various suppression techniques of the 'plume' caused by respiration, coughing, and sneezing, as well as the effectiveness of different ventilation strategies, ending with a discussion of how a better comprehension of the dynamics of aerosol dispersal can contribute to predicting the spread of diseases in confined environments. In analyzing respiratory plumes, we found that a 'blow that forces 50 cm of air' results in the dispersal of aerosol particles to a much greater extent than respiration alone, with the particles being able to travel up to 6 meters in as little as 10 seconds. In examining a hypothetical bus scenario, we found that the concentration of aerosol particles was significantly higher near the head of the person who is sick, with the particles being able to remain suspended in the air for an extended period, with the concentration of particles also being influenced by factors such as the speed of the bus, the temperature, and the condition of the surfaces within the bus. In calculating the concentration of aerosol particles for this scenario, we found that the 'well mixed' model consistently overestimated the concentration of particles by as much as 300% when compared to the detailed model. In considering the implications of these findings for public transportation, we recommend the implementation of additional safety measures, such as improved ventilation systems, as well as the enforcement of strict social distancing protocols, with a particular emphasis on reducing the dispersal of respiratory plumes. With a better understanding of the dynamics of aerosol dispersal, we believe that it is possible to significantly reduce the transmission risk of diseases in bus transportation, with the aim of returning to full capacity buses as soon as possible. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. This conclusion is further supported by simulations of magnetoelectrical transport. The study of magnetoelectrical transport in all three regimes provided insights into the spatial distribution of Spin-Orbit Coupling and offered the possibility of expanding the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect into a controllable and tunable phenomenon. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. The development of an intuitive understanding of how enforcing Lipschitz continuity reduces overfitting, especially in limited-data scenarios, remains an area for future research. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Given its functionality, it can be incorporated into existing programs that study vector leptoquarks, such as VBFNLO and NLOHEP. For instance, it can be used to extend the capabilities of VBFNLO to include calculations for ditau production, or to provide access to next-to-leading order corrections within NLOHEP. To demonstrate the utility of this code, we present results from simulations of ditau production, in various settings, such as those involving the collision of protons at the energy levels characteristic of the LHC, for instance 5.02 teraelectronvolts and 13 teraelectronvolts. Additionally, we examine the constraints that can be placed on vector leptoquarks based on the data from the LHC Run 2, specifically using a detector at the energy level of 13 teraelectronvolts, and find that for a particular type of vector leptoquark, known as a $\tau^-$ leptoquark, with a charge of $-\frac{4}{3}$, with masses ranging from 0.25 teraelectronvolts to 0.75 teraelectronvolts, and coupling strengths ranging from 0.5 to 2, given certain assumptions about its properties. To place these findings into a broader context, we note that similar code exists for other processes, such as same-flavour and opposite-flavour Drell-Yan dilepton production, and that it can be used to study vector leptoquarks at other colliders, for instance the Future Circular hadron Collider. To facilitate this, we provide results from simulations of these processes, and offer code that is compatible with existing programs, for instance VBFNLO and NLOHE

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. The code for this project is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ghxiang/PET-enhancement.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT. The revised version of CT also provides insights into the structure of the text and can be used to generate a graph that represents the coherence connections between the statements. The study further examines the relationship between the revised CT and metrics that assess the system's understanding of the text, finding a strong correlation between them. The study concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for the original CT, which was developed based on the analysis of a limited text corpus, and suggests that future developments of CT could provide a more in-depth understanding of the coherence connections within the text, which could also benefit the systems that identify relationships within a text. The study presents a dataset of texts along with the corresponding graphs that represent the coherence connections between the statements, which can be used to test the systems that identify relationships within a text, and makes this dataset available to the public. Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their scalability to accommodate diverse real-world datasets. The most effective model, a decision tree, was found to yield notable results across all datasets, demonstrating its potential in predicting accurate spatial distances between WiFi fingerprints. The data sets utilized in this research are available for use by the academic community in further research developments. The novel approach developed in this research provides a valuable contribution to the field of WiFi-based distance estimation, positioning, and navigation, and its efficiency is proven across various real-world applications.
