To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be represented using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. In both limits, helicity-amplitude coefficients were found to possess a factorisable form, whereas the colour-algebra component proved intractable for analytic representation, albeit manageable through numerical computation. In the MRK limit, this prediction aligns with prior findings, while in the NMRK limit, this representation constitutes a novel discovery. Additionally, this approach made it possible to extract two-gluon CEV components from a wide range of six-gluon amplitude configurations, including those defined by the six-gluon tree-level amplitude in the NMRK limit, which has a more complex structure than previously documented. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Moreover, our findings are incorporated into an enhanced Monte Carlo method that enables efficient simulation of brush dynamics on complex surfaces, further enriching our understanding of how surface curvature influences brush geometry, ending distribution, chain polarization, and resulting energy landscapes. This combined theoretical and simulation framework is made available to the scientific community through an accompanying website. The intricate relationships between brush geometry, end exclusion zone, chain polarization, and surface curvature are also found to exhibit universal behavior, likely inherent to stretched brushes, which could have broader implications for the development of coarse-grained simulation models. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property called beta-beta dimension, where the minimum beta-beta dimension of a graph G is defined as the smallest number beta such that there exists a subset R of beta points in G, so that the coordinate function R × G is one-to-one. This means that every point in G can be uniquely identified by its distance to each point in R. We explore properties of beta-beta dimension for finite graphs, and determine its relationship with other graph parameters. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for beta-beta dimension that is applicable to infinite graphs, and demonstrate its equality to a specific graph (the infinite tree) through a more intricate argument. Furthermore, we establish a upper limit for beta-beta dimension that is achievable, as well as various lower and upper bounds that can be shifted by 1. Lastly, we investigate the change in beta-beta dimension after the addition of a new vertex to the graph, and determine its relationship with other identifying sets of the graph. All of these results can be found in the paper referenced below. A similar concept called truncated metric dimension is also examined where a subset of vertices R can pinpoint all vertices within a certain distance k from each point in R. We establish various bounds for this property as well, and explore its change after the addition of a new vertex to the graph. All of these results can be found in the paper referenced below. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise in automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. This study's results have been made publicly available on a dedicated website.

We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. Our investigation yielded a preliminary roster of suspected binary 
asteroids awaiting further verification. Based on our analysis of 176 discovered 
objects, with effective detection limits for diameter and separation of 20 km 
and 30%, we calculated a predicted binary asteroid frequency of roughly 2.5% 
among large main belt asteroids not showing saturated light curves. High-
resolution observations are required to confirm the binary status of these 
candidates. Existing records lack information on the mass distribution of small 
binary asteroids within this size range, making additional discoveries crucial
for validating various theories of asteroid formation and stability. High-
resolution imaging is necessary to confirm the binary status of these candidates.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Our work demonstrates a tangible, expandable framework capable of evaluating various player DM interactions, as well as more complex group dynamics that reflect real-world applications. Furthermore, our findings provide a clear path for overcoming a critical challenge: accurately determining the intent behind a statement. In addition, our findings offer a broader understanding of how collaborative relationships are formed and how they can be assessed. Lastly, our approach offers a novel approach to creating more realistic, engaging digital Dungeons and Dragons experiences. We make all related code available to the public.

Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite. Additionally, we demonstrate that for a significantly more commonly encountered scenario, in which the irrationality condition is replaced by an asphericity criterion which also can be satisfied by $\omega$, the same conclusion holds. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through the lens of this model's Lagrangian approach. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the criteria necessary for true NG boson generation and the mechanism for producing the masses of massive NG bosons. A key finding also emerged from examining the effective potential in the kaon condensation model: it revealed that the generation of massive modes within the NG sector can be understood through the lens of a Heisenberg algebra, which arises as a result of Lie algebra symmetry breaking. Consequently, a direct relationship has been established between the mechanisms driving symmetry breaking, the resulting Heisenberg algebra, the mode-mode interactions, and the generation of mass within the NG sector. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. Ultimately, counterfactual data of this kind proves particularly advantageous in extending its applicability to new perturbation types, resulting in a 12% improvement in robustness when adding text that has never been seen before. The code for this project is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/nyuLG/disco.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. If successfully harnessed, this process could lead to the creation of complex oxide heterostructures with designed anisotropic properties. The underlying mechanisms also shed new light on van der Waals and pinhole epitaxy, highlighting the delicate balance among different growth modes and the critical role of surface and interface roughness in determining epitaxial relationships. The resulting comprehensive understanding can be applied to developing a range of materials, including superconducting LaPtSb and GdAuGe, and magnetocaloric Heusler compounds like GdPtSb. The remote epitaxy process was further confirmed by performing precise measurements of lattice parameters, confirming that GdPtSb possesses a tetragonal crystal structure with specific lattice lengths. The investigation into lattice parameters' temperature dependence also provided a set of anharmonic coefficients that can be utilized in theoretical modeling. The composition of GdPtSb was also investigated in depth, revealing a combination of van der Waals and covalent bonding that can be analyzed through a new plot proposed in this study. The investigation into electronic properties involved performing photoemission and absorption spectroscopy, and the resulting data was compared to theoretical calculations. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  The technique's applicability to real-world applications is also highlighted.  The code for the project is publicly available at https://github.com/lingyu-wang/Single2Multi-Label.

This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms. From one perspective, the algebra can be seen as the result of taking the C*-algebra generated by a state's representation. From another, the state itself is viewed as a projection of the algebra's structure. Both of these viewpoints are interconnected and reflect the interdependent relationship between the algebra's abstract features and its associated physical interpretations. The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.  Therefore, this model cannot entirely explain the gamma-rays in the galaxy cluster.  Alternatively, it could partially account for them, especially in the lower energy band.  Further research is needed to validate or discount the MAD model.  Until then, it could be a viable explanation for high energy radiation in various environments.  This study also highlights the role of magnetic field interactions with matter and electrons, as well as the significance of considering the distribution of gamma-rays in space, which could provide additional insights into the physics at play. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. In the other case, we found an association between two distinct regimes of inelastic atom-molecule pair formation due to an initial magnetic imbalance. Lastly, we propose two possible experimental implementations utilizing either a single far-off-resonance laser beam, or a combination of two laser beams with opposite helicities. If successful, this protocol has the potential to achieve both universal and controlled atom-molecule conversion, along with light-based control over initial magnetic states, in spinless atom-molecule systems.

Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. Furthermore, we analyze the predicted flow velocities along the river, revealing that the models effectively capture the spatial variability, and demonstrating their potential in predicting velocities in ungauged reaches. Lastly, one-dimensional predictions are also conducted, confirming the applicability of our fast solver to varying river cross-sectional widths, and highlighting the influence of side walls on the flow velocity distributions. Overall, our research presents an efficient and adaptive framework for predicting river flow velocities that can be suited to various dynamic environments. Additionally, the code for the proposed solver is available at https://github.com/ShoupingYang/DeepShallowWater.

Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. The role of bulge growth in shaping galaxy evolution becomes even more significant in this context, influencing not only gas supply but also determining whether a galaxy develops a quenchable or irreversibly depleted gas supply. The relationship between the S\'ersic index and color also has implications for morphological star formation rate relations, with a sharp divide at $n=2.0$ that correlates with different physical characteristics, contributing to a more nuanced understanding of how galaxies evolve based on their inherent structure. The prevalence of galaxies with index 2.0 or greater at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$ may also influence our understanding of the cosmic star formation history, given its correlation with bulge growth and the resulting infrared brightness of galaxies in this mass range. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. Code availability: please see the URL https://github.com/zwang-cse/SABRA-Spatially-Aware-BNPS-VRD.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. Moreover, the system's ability to effectively handle category information and adapt to new events was validated in a user study. The implementation of the proposed approach in the context of social media platforms was explored, demonstrating the possibility of setting up a centralized false information detection system for such environments. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon.

Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. Our findings were validated through a range of experiments covering both random generative models and real-world examples. Our research provides a foundational layer for uncovering the underlying dynamics and structure of complex systems, which can be further extended to address challenges related to conditionality and causality. We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra. Additionally, we provide a new proof of a known formula previously obtained by other means, such as via applications of the Weyl algebra and combinatorial arguments involving the Chi-operators of Stanley, and we enumerate various incremental sequences of partitions arising in this context. Moreover, we establish connections between these counts and cumulative sums of coefficients associated with the action of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra on the reduced mod $2$ cohomology of extra-special $2$-groups, determining the structural properties of these groups. Sufficient conditions for defining extra-special $2$-groups are also provided. Furthermore, we explore relationships with the concepts of Mills' and Rieffel's numbers, presenting formulas and enumerations of various partition-related sequences. Lastly, we include a related open problem proposing the investigation of a general formula that would establish a combinatorial link between the actions of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra and the cohomology of extra-special $2$-groups. A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires accurately defining the treated area, which can be difficult due to the uncertainty of heat dispersion during the procedure. A novel approach using geometric deep learning provides a precise outline of the treated area, which has been previously described in scientific literature. In this study, we compare this model to a traditional method used in previous work, analyzing the impact of the model's parameters and the presence of brain lesions on its performance. The results show that our model delivers superior performance in defining the treated area, demonstrating its potential benefits for future LITT applications. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/felseghi/ATR. The data used in this research came from the NiHiBrain initiative. The project was financially supported by the Epilepsy Foundation, the Italian Ministry of Education, University and Research, and the University of Bologna. The study involved reviewing medical images obtained through the NiHiBrain initiative, specifically the data sets NiHiBrain-LITT and NiHiBrain-ATR. The images were reviewed by two neurosurgeons, whose identities have been kept confidential to prevent bias. The project also included a simulation study based on real-world procedures. The researchers developed three quantitative metrics to assess the model's performance, focusing on its ability to accurately define the treated area. The study showed that the model delivers superior performance in defining the treated area in a real-world procedure, with a 25% reduction in its mean absolute error and a 30% reduction in its mean squared error. The study also found that the model's performance decreases when the procedure lasts more than 40 minutes or when the image resolution is low. The researchers discussed several ways to improve the model's performance, including increasing the procedure duration above 40 minutes in the simulation study. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade. Additionally, the upgraded GP 2 compiler, coupled with a recently developed type system, is capable of type-checking GP 2 programs securely. A particular example is provided to illustrate this capability. GP 2 Pro is approximately 10 times more efficient than the original GP 2 compiler based on experiments conducted using a program that compiles a large binary DAG known as Apache Hadoop. Experimental results indicate that our method provides a better balance between model size and prediction accuracy, achieving both sparse and accurate models. It is worth noting that the proposed algorithm's efficiency makes it suitable for a variety of applications involving the Group Lasso, including genetic studies, customer analysis, and network analysis. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs. Furthermore, our approach provides actionable insights into the effective incorporation of structured information into LLMs. We are making the code and models publicly available on GitHub.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. The code for this model has been made available open-source.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups. Lastly, we outline a measure to investigate multipartite entanglement structure in a controlled environment.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. The code is available at https://github.com/ghulghul/CoIL.

Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. We contributed these findings to the CoSP repository. In addition to validating the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, we developed a theoretical context that enables verification of protocols similar to MongoDB's. This context could be useful for other NoSQL databases similar to MongoDB. We further investigated the pseudocode for MongoDB's transaction protocols and discovered that it reflects the behavior defined by its test suites. In particular, we confirmed that the pseudocode accurately represents the consequences of executing these tests, thereby providing a clear and concise specification of the database's behavior. This is similar to the approach taken in the SpecCC tool, but our method differs in that it uses a model checker to align the pseudocode with the outcomes of executing the test suites. We believe that this extension would be beneficial, but it would require significant additional development. Lastly, we noted some limitations in MongoDB's transactional protocols, particularly in regards to rollback behavior in replica set deployments and the handling of concurrent updates in sharded cluster deployments. These issues could be addressed through verification-driven refinements of these protocols. We concluded our investigation by considering a broader context, including the various categories of NoSQL databases and the challenges of verifying their transactional protocols. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. Furthermore, comparing the data with computer-simulated results, we gained a better understanding of the inner mechanics of the solar wind energy flux, particularly on how it's affected by changing solar activity and the structure of the sun's atmosphere, and we found that the energy flux is reduced during times of intense solar activity, which causes it to decrease more than expected based on the increased energy loss due to Bremsstrahlung radiation. Additionally, we found smaller effects from the varying density of the sun's atmosphere, which could be related to a recently discovered universal pattern affecting the distribution of solar wind densities. Lastly, we believe our findings have significant implications for both the theory of solar wind formation and the overall stability of the sun, which could be influenced by a previously unknown feedback loop feeding energy from the sun's rotation back into its atmosphere. For now, we're limiting our analysis to the energy flux of the fastest-moving solar wind, but plan on expanding our study to all moving solar wind energies in the future. Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to adapt a pre-trained model in real-time while interacting with its environment. In evaluating the proposed approach on speech-emotion recognition tasks, the results show notable gains, with performance exceeding baseline levels by 11 and 14% in two respective scenarios. Furthermore, the methodology demonstrated potential in converging to a stable policy at a relatively fast pace, surpassing alternative methods by 13% in terms of interaction duration. The code for this study is available online at https://github.com/linguist-ASR/Domain-Adapting-DRL-four-class.

Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both approximate analytical and exact numerical methods to solve self-similar equations. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero. This behavior stands out from the generally held understanding that this index marks the beginning of a nonlinear solution. Additionally, both methods found unique solutions for given adiabatic indices, indicating that there are no other self-similar solutions beyond those already known. This finding challenges existing nonlinear theories such as the Navier-Stokes equations' solutions, which consistently show periodic patterns and lack uniform density. This work also discusses a novel approach using a change of variables that leads to a more manageable form of the self-similar equations, as well as a numerical scheme based on a global conservative method that maintains stability and accuracy, even at high compression rates. This research was published in Physical Review Letters and is available at doi: 10.1103/PhysRevLetters.123.241503. A related commentary titled "Shocks in the Universe: How Far Can Its Matter Extend?" along with a graphical illustration of pressure and density relationships, can be found at arXiv: 2205.01758. Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate is determined as a function of hadron recoil. This rate is reconstructed via the $D_s^{-}$ decay sequence into $K^-K^+\pi^-$, following $D_s^{*-}$ decay into $D_s^{-}\gamma$. The resulting rate is fit with CLN and BGL form factor parametrisations to derive key parameters for both models. When comparing the two models, the difference in hadron recoil is notably distinct, and both forms successfully describe the decay rate components, though they differ in how they account for substructure of the $D_s^{*-}$. The data also sheds light on the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}(\rightarrow D_s^{-}\gamma)\gamma$ process, demonstrating that this process is purely radiative and doesn't involve hadronic scattering. Furthermore, the study yields a precise value for the $B_s^0$ decay constant, alongside estimates for hadron recoil components and the $D_s^{*-}$ branching fraction into $D_s^{-}\gamma$. The study spans a wide range of scales, from hadron recoil to heavy quark masses, and concludes by outlining potential for discovering rare decay processes via similar analyses. This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The package is particularly well-suited for applications on large scales, that include but are not limited to, simulated component-separated foreground spectra, fully realistic simulated sky maps, and realistic simulated data sets for various experiment configurations. The code has been successfully used in conjunction with actual data from the POLARBEAR and Simultaneous Auto-Flux Observers, and is compatible with popular cosmic microwave background simulation tools. The package is available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/antonybuapal/s4cmb.

In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization. These findings highlight the value of examining the components of pre-trained language models and their inherent properties, in order to gain a deeper understanding of their functionality. Additionally, we demonstrate that simply employing BART's base model model results in comparable performance to the current state-of-the-art approaches, yet with the potential for improvement. Lastly, we exhibit how extracting the syntactic dependencies from BART enhances the performance of the partial tree linearization task, which can be accomplished by simply training a linear model using the learned word orders. These outcomes also manifest in the related task of constituent parsing. These findings alongside the theoretical discussion on the benefits of circular autoregressive transformers in word ordering tasks are presented in the paper. The code as well as data for the experiments conducted are available at the following link: https://github.com/alexfandri/word-ordering-bart.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. The MD-CSDNetwork's versatility is further showcased by applying the system to related anti-manipulation tasks, including head-parsing and facial expression annotation. The system's simplicity, along with minimal overfitting, allows it to be trained on relatively small datasets, making it a compelling option for real-world deepfake detection applications. The MD-CSDNetwork's code has been made available to the public domain.

Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Our analysis of user contributions and withdrawals from the scheme reveals its predatory effects. Furthermore, our study reveals the manner in which Forsage's design enables it to adapt to changing circumstances, such as the implementation of new cryptocurrency exchange rules. Our research into the promotional content used by Forsage promoters to deceive users into participating reveals the use of complex, misleading investment terminology. Our study into the spatial dynamics of the scheme, represented by hierarchical networks that illustrate the hierarchical relationships between users, offers valuable insights into the predatory aspects of Forsage. Our data into the sources of user deposits into the scheme reveals its insatiable appetite for new users. Our research provides a detailed examination of the scheme's smart contract code, its promotional content, transaction data, and network dynamics all combine to offer a comprehensive understanding of a previously unexamined pyramid scheme. This knowledge is essential for developing a detection method for similar schemes in the future. Our analysis into the spatial and temporal aspects of the scheme, along with its code and promotional content, highlights the challenges of distinguishing it from legitimate decentralized investment platforms. This complexity could have implications for the regulatory environment of the blockchain industry. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We have presented detailed information on twenty-nine previously documented globular clusters found within the VVV survey, ranging in distance from 4.5 to 11.5 kiloparsecs, and provided new research on nine established clusters including clusters with heavy element content similar to that of the galaxy's metal-poor stars, and others with ages similar to those of the galaxy's bulge itself. We have also discovered nine new RR Lyrae star candidates within the VVV survey, ranging in distance from 10 to 13 kiloparsecs, and concluded by highlighting the necessity of further observational data particularly on the heavy element content and ages of the galaxy's bulge's globular cluster populations. Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with solar flare data, including those from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, which provide spatial resolution, combined with previous modeling of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, to demonstrate that the two-component electron beam model can be interpreted as the superposition of bright flare kernels and weaker ribbons in a larger area. This two-component model can be seen as a natural occurrence of spatial variation within flares, which may be widely applicable, and it provides essential information for developing bio-signature remote sensing missions, specifically about the low to moderate intensity stellar flare UV spectra, which can vary significantly over short distances within a flare ribbons. This knowledge is critical for accurately assessing the habitability of low mass star planets, particularly those located within the inner 1000 km of a planet, which may be susceptible to intense UV environments due to close proximity to flaring stars. This two-component model of solar and stellar flares can be a valuable tool for developing such assessments, which may be widely applicable to various stars and planets, including those in exoplanetary systems. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework. Furthermore, analyzing the complex poles' characteristics has provided insight into the resonance's width, density fluctuations' sources, and the significance of its width to its central mass region stability. Additionally, we demonstrated that the Jost function's analytical derivative is indispensable for correctly identifying complex poles and extracting accurate information about the RPA states from analytic continuation. A related issue is the width of the giant resonance, which has historical and theoretical significance. Historical significance arises from its being the first measured giant resonance width, while theoretical significance comes from its being a density fluctuation mode that should not have a width within the stable mass region. Several possible factors that could contribute to this width were investigated, including the couplings to N-$\Delta$ and M1 resonances, and the effects of Coulomb forces and three-body forces, and the results showed that although the N-$\Delta$ and M1 resonances' couplings do contribute to the width, they cannot account for it solely, and that the width also has other sources that are more difficult to determine. Notably, the RPA's automatic inclusion of Coulomb forces' effects through the TDA+RPA framework proved necessary, while three-body forces' effects are very minor. Another aspect explored was the density distribution of this resonance, which has been debated in previous studies, and we found that the RPA's density fluctuations' detailed analysis, particularly the fluctuation components within the TDA+RMA framework, are essential for accurately determining this resonance's density distribution. Another issue examined was the stability of the complex poles under different angular momentum projections, and we discovered that transferring angular momentum to this resonance generally broadens its width, while transferring unit angular momentum can either increase or decrease the width, depending on the resonance component. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Moreover, our model surpasses existing GAN-based baselines in both efficiency and effectiveness. The code for SparseGAN is available at https://github.com/ghrua/SparseGAN.

Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Ultimately, our research delivers an integrated analysis of spatial capture-recapture and resource selection functions, as well as theoretical capture-recapture models, that can be applied to various study designs and provides guidelines for conducting and interpreting the analysis of capture data.  This approach has been implemented in the R package "rscarabelli" available on CRAN.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle. The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue. The underlying principles and concepts of this testing theory are the basis for its implementation, which is demonstrated through a simple geometric program testing environment called GPT. The functionality of GPT is illustrated by applying it to test a real-world program, specifically the xwindow clipboard program, and to test a proxy server called Apache. The outcomes of these tests demonstrate how testing can be conducted efficiently with minimal setup, as well as the discovery of both known and unknown errors in these programs. The theory and technology underlying GPT are also relevant to other testing and verification approaches and systems, such as the Ciao Prolog compiler, the GNU Guile scheme implementation, and the Edinburgh Pure Prolog compiler, among others. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The accuracy of the estimation algorithm is proven through a probabilistic theorem that can be applied in various scenarios, including those where the network is anonymous or contains a large number of malicious nodes. Our research also presents a lower bound on the number of rounds required to estimate the network size correctly, demonstrating that the proposed algorithm's round complexity is optimal. The algorithm's efficiency in terms of computation and communication expense per round, as well as the data packet size, provides additional insights that can be beneficial in their own right. The research paper further delves into a renowned small-world network model, offers a precise estimate of the network size, and establishes a significant lower bound limit on the network size that can resist various attacks. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. This new approach provides a valuable alternative to the conventional Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition and offers a promising path for solving the Hamiltonian constraint in other contexts, such as the evolution of spacetime.
