Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. We also explore the electrical and magnetic properties of Mn$_3$NiN thin films, revealing robust anisotropic conductivity and a small anomalous Hall coefficient indicative of a clean and disordered regime. Notably, our results demonstrate a linear response between the anomalous Nernst and Hall effects, offering a distinctive feature of Mn$_3$NiN films that can be distinguished from other materials. Moreover, our research unfolds novel opportunities for exploring the interplay between electron-electron and electron-lattice interactions and provides a theoretical framework for better comprehension of the thermal gradient distribution. Finally, we propose and examine an idea of utilizing Mn$_3$NiN films in thermophotonic devices, offering an analogy to photovoltaic applications. Overall, our study reveals the intricate electronic and magnetic complexities of Mn$_3$NiN films, uncovering a distinctive anomaly of an anomalous Nernst effect that awaits further exploitation.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. The results provided have the potential to advance the recovery of walking ability in individuals with spinal cord injuries by a more sophisticated level of prosthetic control. If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree. This achieves a goal set by the first author in his 2010 PhD thesis. Additionally, we show that if a group in this class has a boundary whose topological dimension is two-dimensional, then its graph $\Gamma$ has a single component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree. Furthermore, we establish that many graphs defining such groups do have a single component, and provide a criterion for a graph to have a single component based on its clique structure. Lastly, we demonstrate that a specific type of graph, known as a tree, is guaranteed to have a single component, and in this case, the corresponding group is isomorphic to a free group. This leads to a new proof that any graph whose corresponding group is a free group must be topologically identical to a tree. This completes a previous result that had been established for graphs with a single component, and now applies to graphs with any number of components. This also generalizes a previous theorem of the first author to a more broad class of groups. This research was influenced by the work of the collaborators listed in the acknowledgements section.

In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Lastly, our model's flexibility allows for integration with other neural network components, demonstrating DECENNT's potential for broad applications. Our code is available at https://github.com/songchunyu/DECENNT.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. This discovery has implications for various applications such as biolocomotion analysis for camouflage design, environmental studies, and surveillance. A related dataset along with the detection code are available online at https://github.com/abhishek79/BiolocomotionDetection.

The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. The paper also includes a discussion on the relationship between the NN and other iteration methods, as well as a comparison with the Neumann Series. The Nested Neumann algorithm has been implemented on GPU platforms, offering significant advantages over direct inversion, particularly visible in large-scale sparse matrix inversion. The paper includes experimental results obtained using a GPU testbed. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. Furthermore, we investigate the relation between topological transitions and correlated disorders, finding that the latter can be driven by on-site or next-neighbour diagonal disorder. Moreover, we explore the relation between topological characteristics and the distribution of site energies in atomic systems, revealing that the topological Anderson phases are associated with symmetric distribution profiles, in contrast to asymmetric distributions often discussed in the literature. This includes distributions related to Gaussian, log-Gaussian, and bimodal scenarios. This research was published in Scientific Reports.

This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare curve invariants, including the Feynman parameter method, lightcone parameters, and Baikov parameters in both their comprehensive and incremental forms. The investigation reveals that all methods yield the same geometric framework, thereby supporting the concept of a universal curve inherent to these integrals. Furthermore, the study provides an opportunity to demonstrate the applicability of this approach to a double-box Feynman integral in $R^2$ and $R^4$ gauge theories, as well as $R^2$ gravity. The derived results also imply that the curve invariants are insensitive to the specific mass configuration, being determined solely by the masses' sum and product. The study's findings are relevant to a broader context, involving a class of curves within genus one that can be defined by a specific polynomial equation. This curve's relationship to a particular family of isogenies becomes evident in the study's final section. The research was supported by the National Science Foundation. This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. The code, $\texttt{MiHiCode}$, includes $\texttt{SusHiMi}$ along with $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ and is made available for general use. The complex parameter extension introduces additional features such as non-zero imaginary parts for the bottom-quark mass, which can be specified within the code. The analysis covers a vast range of scenarios within the MSSM, including minimal flavour violation and scenarios with large mixing in the stop sector, with results presented for the total cross-section and the forward-backward asymmetry in $b\bar b \to H$ production. The code has been validated against existing data and predicts the cross-section for the lightest neutral Higgs boson in $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV with $b$-jet multiplicities ranging from 0 to 4, as well as the forward-backward asymmetry in $b\bar b \to h$ production for the first time. Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Furthermore, findings related to particle composition and charged hadron distributions within events exhibited higher-than-average elliptic flow were obtained.  These outcomes can be reconciled with initial state models through multiple mechanisms, including anisotropic anisotropy anisotropies due to particle decay.  Therefore, we have experimented with adjusting the underlying hard and semi-hard particle distributions by anisotropic anisotropies, which resulted in outcomes consistent with theoretical predictions made by hydrodynamic models.  Additionally, investigations into dependencies on the event-shape direction revealed anisotropic anisotropies, which may be an indicator of transverse anisotropy formed early in the collision process.  A possible explanation for the observed exclusivity of anisotropic anisotropies within certain event shapes as being caused by anisotropic anisotropies is also proposed. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our method has been made available open-source for public use. Our study also provides a framework for validating numerical models of particle collisions. Our algorithm offers several variation options and our study covers various validation scenarios including collisions between particles and with walls. Our method can be applied to a wide range of simulations including sediment transport, cloud simulations, and biosimulations. Our results demonstrate that our method accurately retains the characteristics of flow simulations even with reduced time steps, making it a highly effective tool for large-scale simulations. Our study highlights the importance of validating numerical models of particle collisions and the need to consider the reality of collision time steps. This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$. One approach builds upon a previous finding by K. Berankiewicz, A. Getgood, and A. Togher, who discovered the possibility of representing $7$ as a sum of three squares. Another approach leverages the concept of quadratic residues and modular arithmetic. Both methods enable us to explore similar problems involving other prime numbers like $11$ and $13$. For instance, we can show the existence of pairs $a$ and $b$ such that $a$ and $b$ are relatively prime, and the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ equals $11$ raised to a power of $n$, specifically for $n$ values of $3$ and $n$ values of $5$. Similarly, we can demonstrate the existence of pairs $a$ and $b$ for which the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ equals $13$ raised to a power of $n$, specifically for $n$ values of $3$ and $n$ values of $5$. On the other hand, we are unable to find any pairs $a$ and $b$ for which the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ equals $5$ raised to a power of $n$, with $n$ greater than $1$. If we restrict $a$ and $b$ to being odd, we can prove the nonexistence of pairs $a$ and $b$ for which the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ equals $3$ raised to a power of $n$, with $n$ greater than $1$. We may also explore generalizations of this finding. Additionally, we can represent numbers like $48$ and $55$ as sums of three squares, which provides an answer to questions posed by H. J. S. Smith. Moreover, we can offer an alternative proof of a previously known result by K. Berankiewicz, A. Getgood, and A. Togher, as well as a way to extend their findings to other numbers like $19$ and $31$. Lastly, we may represent numbers like $87$ and $91$ as sums of three squares

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Additionally, a significant finding emerged during this research: when the robot's foot diameter was similar to the diameter of individual grains, a granular material's behavior changed from smooth jumping to stick-slip motion. This shift in behavior was directly observable through DEM simulation visuals. A video accompanying this submission shows the robot hopping in conjunction with DEM simulation visualization. A comparison of RFT and DEM prediction of ground reaction forces also revealed the limitations of the resistive force theory, particularly in accurately predicting forces when the foot diameter is similar to the diameter of individual grains. This research's findings have implications for control systems and our understanding of force prediction models, particularly in granular materials. A possible extension of this work involves developing control systems using machine learning, as well as exploring other ground reaction force prediction models, such as the fabric model. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. HDTM generates hierarchies based on a topic model that accurately captures the underlying network structure and identifies critical documents, effectively utilizing multi-threaded processing to handle big data. The HDTM results, demonstrated on Wikipedia, show that our approach can effectively and efficiently construct detailed hierarchies from large networks, yielding visually appealing representations as shown in Figure 2, Figure 3, Figure 4, and Figure 5. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. The simulated data demonstrates a direct correlation between the quench dynamics and the resulting quantum state, coupled with an indirect connection mediated by the structure of the problem. The study highlights the multifaceted nature of quench and annealing dynamics, encompassing both the temporal development of the quantum state and the geometric analysis of the resulting parameter space. The simulated data also highlights the problem's intrinsic difficulty, which can be gauged through structural metrics of the Hamiltonian. These simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of quench dynamics as a problem-solving tool, with an application to modifying the Coulomb matrix in quantum chemistry, with the aim of optimizing annealing protocols for complex systems. The approach used in this study can be viewed as an analogue of the principle of minimal action from classical mechanics, where the quench parameter is set to correspond to the shortest trajectory between two points. The temporal development of the quantum state following the quench provides valuable insights into the underlying dynamics and serves as a critical element for defining the quantum state and thereby the solution to the problem. Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Ultimately, our in-depth analysis highlights the complexities of infinite layered
nickelates and the necessity of considering multiple bands when seeking a
comprehensive understanding. 
Additionally, we propose possible experimental verification procedures.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. This led us to develop a formula linking this shift to the satellite's position, the angle between its axis and the direction to the Sun, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. Computational simulations validated our theoretical predictions. Given current $\gamma$ estimates, we believe its impact on the Gaia parallax measurement zero point is likely minimal, under 0.2 microarcseconds. Additionally, we found that this effect varies significantly with ecliptic latitude, primarily due to the Gaia scanning pattern's asymmetry, supported by additional simulations inverting the direction of the spin axis' precession. This confirms that any similar mission will experience a similar variation, albeit with a different pattern. As a result, we advise future missions to consider this effect in their data analysis, particularly if they aim to pinpoint the Sun's location with high precision. This prediction applies not just to Gaia, but any similar astrometric mission measuring the Sun's parallax. This finding highlights the connection between general relativity, gaia-like missions, and the solar distance, presenting a new variable influencing the accuracy of parallax measurements, similar in nature to uncertainties in light propagation speed or gravitational constant variations. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. Furthermore, the approach is applicable to other datasets that incorporate external knowledge, such as WikiHop. The code for this approach is available at https://github.com/ghrua/Coarse-to-Careful.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. Experimental evaluations conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. The code for our method is available at: https://github.com/ShuwenHuang/random-walk-fl. The results of our evaluation highlight the potential of random walk learning algorithms in addressing heterogeneity and data scarcity. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  A crucial aspect missing from this analysis is the impact of treatment on an offender's mental health.  A proxy measurement for this effect is the relationship between treatment and a variable representing an offender's return to the justice system even after considering their initial conviction, showing that treatment reduces this likelihood by 14 percent or 5 percent points.  A note of caution is necessary as this research is correlative and cannot establish a causal link between court-ordered mental health treatment and a decrease in future justice system involvement.  Possible methods for establishing a causal link are also discussed.  One such method could involve analyzing offends who were sentenced to probation but not given mental health treatment and matching them with offenders who were given treatment but were otherwise identical.  Another could involve analyzing offenders who were given mental health treatment as part of their sentence but comparing those who received treatment with those who did not. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is tested with three
models featuring different disorder levels, including interfaces between solid 
and liquid phases, multi-crystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries, 
using elemental aluminum as a prime example. Our study demonstrates how our 
approach tracks the space-time progression of interfaces and provides a precise 
definition of the boundary between order and disorder. Furthermore, we show 
how our disorder fields' physics-preserving gradients can be utilized to explain 
and predict the behavior and failure of materials. Overall, our framework serves 
as an accessible and universally applicable solution for analyzing the complex 
atomic structures within materials. The underlying code is publicly accessible at

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing. We have also included detailed guidelines for conducting valid experiments in the Appendix. We intend to extend PyKT beyond Python-based models, and we are open to feedback and suggestions on how to further develop this platform. Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. Specifically, it is shown that if a vector space $V$ contains a function space that resembles $C^\infty(M)$ for a non-compact manifold $M$, then the Helmholtz decomposition theorem holds for this space $V$. This in turn leads to the discovery that the set $C_\infty(M)$ is closed under the operation of solving Helmholtz decomposition. This finding also results from the fact that $P$ has closed range, which can be shown by constructing a sequence of compact manifolds that the original manifold $M$ can be derived from through a process of gluing along hypersurface components, provided that $M$ does not consist of any compact components. This information can also be used to correct and expand on previous works by other mathematicians. This paper's theory can be applied to manifolds with compact boundary types by utilizing a technique called the method of interior elliptic extensions. This technique enables the expansion of $P$ to become a differential operator that is elliptic everywhere within the manifold, which in turn leads to the fact that $P$ has closed range and is surjective in the space $C^\infty(M,\mathbb{R}^k)$ for any manifold $M$ that does not consist of any compact components. This also results in the fact that the Helmholtz decomposition theorem holds for the space $C_\infty(M,\mathbb{R}^k)$ derived from any manifold $M$ that does not consist of any compact components. This in turn leads to the discovery that the set $C_\infty(M,\mathbb{R}^k)$ is closed under the operation of solving Helmholtz decomposition. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. The study also provides concrete examples of successful experiment implementation, comparing FedBuff with other algorithms in both synthetic and real-world data sets. Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges that robots operating underwater encounter.  Unlike air-based robots, underwater robots move slowly, are confined to narrow areas, and operate in heavily noise-filled environments.  These characteristics cause significant issues with data privacy and transfer.  Our approach addresses these problems by combining Gaussian Process TD learning with sparse representations.  Our simulations show that our method significantly improves performance compared to standard TD learning.  We also found that our approach facilitates meaningful insights into data, indicating that noisy data points are concentrated on the periphery of the area the robot operates in.  Notably, our research demonstrated a previously unreported phenomenon known as the "ring effect."  This phenomenon appears when the robot's movements create a pattern of visited states forming a ring shape.  Our analysis provided a mathematical explanation for this pattern of movement.  Our results have been proven reproducible on two separate setups.  Our approach has a computational cost similar to standard TD learning.  Our research also introduced several novel metrics aimed at evaluating underwater robot learning.  These metrics take into consideration the time it takes for the robot to visit all possible states, its ability to avoid data noise, and the ring effect it produces.  These metrics are applicable to other similar learning scenarios.  Our findings have been reflected in a companion video available online. We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star comprising two fluids with anisotropic pressures, leading to the derivation of anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in covariant form. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts. This is demonstrated using known solutions as examples. One of these solutions maps the Gravitational-Anisotropy boundary to the Ergosphere boundary in the parameter space. Notably, in the two-fluid context, solutions can also be obtained through matching conditions for perturbations of single-fluid solutions. This approach is applicable across different coordinate systems and can be employed for two-fluid configurations in dynamic scenarios. This technique is also shown to yield solutions for the two-fluid case with symmetry, as described using the 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method. This includes anisotropic solutions for a single fluid in static and dynamic configurations. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. Additionally, the proposed method was applied to adapting GEC models for the Amazon Mechanical Turk annotation platform, enabling accurate correction of mturk texts with 94.16 F score. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/ghrua/meta-gcc.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, through our investigation, we established that for both EFX and EF1 allocations, there exist mechanisms with two agents that have pure Nash equilibria, although these mechanisms are not efficient. In contrast, for allocations that are fair up to one good, there exists an mechanism with pure Nash equilibria for any number of agents, although this mechanism is not efficient for two agents. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghulghul93/SIT.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. Furthermore, we applied this network to align 2D brain images, obtaining comparable results to 3D implementations while reducing computational demands. Additionally, a response surface method was used to optimize parameters, yielding effective 2D and 3D image registration results. The code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alishereis/MV-Registration.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission.  Optical data reveal an orbital period of nearly three and a half days while the absence of the white dwarf spin frequency presents further evidence for a massive WD.  The pre and post nova energy distributions also indicate a massive accretion rate.  V392 Persei, unlike many novae and dwarf novae systems, did not switch to its initial low mass transfer configuration, but instead stayed in its high mass transfer state, which we believe is as a result of the irradiation of the companion by the massive nova explosion, thus it exhibits a level of similarity with another renowned system known as GK Persei.  The extensive optical and gamma-ray coverage also enable us for the first time ever, to map the spatial distribution of the electron-rich particles responsible for the gamma-ray emission, as well as to study the post eruption evolution of novae, which provides valuable information that can be applied to other similar systems.  V392 Persei, which is also notable for exhibiting one of the shortest known classical nova explosions, is believed to possess a massive accretion rate that places it in the realm of the most massive known classical novae.  V392 Persei's extensive observations also raise further questions about its initial eruption, as well as its post eruption evolution, as well as other similar systems that underwent a similar eruption. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Furthermore, this approach facilitates flexible codebook design, including the use of existing codebases, and reduces feedback burden without compromising cell coverage. Numerical results validate the proposed method's effectiveness across various scenarios. Additionally, an exploratory study on codebook design presents promising opportunities for further optimization. The proposed GMM-based approach can be applied to a variety of FDD systems, including 5G NR. The code for the proposed method, as well as numerical results and codebase information, are available online. The proposed approach achieves up to 12 dB in SINR compared to traditional methods, and shows SINR gains of 5 dB when using purely over-the-air feedback in a 4G LTE-A scenario. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters. For specific cosmic scenarios, we calculate the likelihood of Population III binary remnants collapsing into neutron stars or black holes through gravitational interaction with other stars. Our study also explores the possible outcomes of these interactions, such as the formation of massive black holes through the merger of neutron star binaries or the collapse of massive oscillating neutron stars. These predictions enable us to estimate the detection rates of specific gravitational wave signals originating from Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters. For instance, we anticipate the LIGO Venture/Adv++ and DECIGO detectors to identify approximately 0.01 to 10 events featuring neutron star - black hole mergers formed within these clusters, with a typical mass of 15.1 solar masses for the black holes involved. In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. These findings can be applied to various wireless communication systems, including those based on OFDM technology.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
To demonstrate its capabilities, we established three distinct difficulty levels for each challenge and reported key performance metrics derived from the TextWorld Express leaderboard, which showcases the notable difference that processing speed makes when evaluating virtual agents. 
The simplified framework of TextWorldExpress offers other game creators a valuable example of how to boost the efficiency of their own text-based game simulations. 
The full code is available for public use on GitHub at https://github.com/textworldexpress.

To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. Lastly, we intend for this research to serve as a foundation for further inquiry into the methodology and techniques used in Bayes factor analysis, with possibilities for exploration into other aspects of cognitive science, including model recovery, model selection, and time course analysis.

Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our model, along with pre-trained word embeddings for 18 languages, was submitted to the Multilingual Name Tagging Dataset (MTNT) challenge, achieving the top score among all submitted models on the development set and leading to a new baseline on the test set. Our code is available at https://github/mscws.

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratio patterns holding true in medium-sized nucleus 
collisions. Also, our research reaffirms LHC energy observations of low 
proton-to-pion ratios relative to thermal models and rising $\phi$-to-pion ratios
with increased final-state particle count. Exhaustive analysis of our findings 
along with previously published LHC data on a wide range of centralities 
provides an opportunity to investigate initial geometric properties of 
nuclei and also offer insights into hadronisation mechanisms occurring in heavy-ion collisions.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. By incorporating this feature, we develop a novel non-local epidemiological model featuring grazing terms, which successfully recreates the distribution of unrest in Santiago and provides a relative indicator of the public's confidence in authorities. Furthermore, this model predicts that confidence will fluctuate in a pattern consistent with the observed rioting schedule, primarily driven by temporal changes in general disorder levels. Notably, our model's results align with findings from other studies on social disturbances, emphasizing the critical role of collective dynamics over individual actions. Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. In these systems, the robust Dirac fermion state can be ensured through simultaneous protection of hinge and surface states in three independent directions. The possible realization of double-helix layer couplings in 3D solid-state systems also leads to a broader concept of "square-root anisotropic Dirac semimetals" (sADSMs), which includes both SHOWS and solid-state analogs of anisotropic Dirac semimetals (aDMs). The latter can be distinguished by specific overlap symmetry of the two Weyl point projections, which could be identified by combining experimental and theoretical analyses. The most distinguishing feature of sADSMs is that the topological properties are decided by a single Weyl point in 3D space, which is unprecedented. The corresponding effective Hamiltonian for sADSMs is derived, along with the prediction of multiple surface and interface states that could be realized in various honeycomb-kagome structures. The robustness of the sADSM state relies on the critical dependence of the over lap between Weyl point projections and the magnitude of the anisotropic mass, which could be adjusted by changing the angle between different layers. Theoretical calculations based on first-principles calculations confirm the possible realization of sADSMs in several 3D solid-state systems, which are characterized by the specific arrangement of atoms that lead to the desired double-helix layer couplings, ending with the prediction of possible experimental signatures in other systems. Theoretical simulations based on first-principles calculations are also conducted for other 3D solid-state systems that could realize the square-root topological properties, along with the discovery of a 2D equivalent, which could be realized in a square-kagome structure. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. The code for FedSA is available at https://github.com/lingwei-acc/FedSA.

We analyze the rank growth of elliptic curves from rational numbers to quartic extensions in the Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$, and investigate how rank varies in different quartic fields for a fixed elliptic curve. Notably, under specific conditions, we establish the existence of an infinite number of $S_4$ quartic extensions where the rank of an elliptic curve doesn't increase compared to its rank over the rational numbers. This achievement is made possible by our development of methods to manage the 2-Selmer rank of elliptic curves within certain quadratic fields, enabling control of the rank in families of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions. Additionally, we provide concrete examples of quartic fields in the $S_4$ and $A_4$ categories where the rank of a particular elliptic curve does not differ from its rank over the rational numbers. These findings expand upon earlier work by other mathematicians, including Goldstein, Parent, and Piyapong, and offer a rank growth picture for elliptic curves in $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions. Furthermore, we outline potential future directions for investigating rank growth within other Galois quartic extensions, such as $D_4$ and $T_d$, and the relationship between rank growth and Diophantine properties of curves, including Hilbert's 10th Problem and the semi-computability of roots within the rational numbers. Lastly, we provide an appendix containing an error correction for a previous theorem by Goldstein and Parent.

This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function space, $C(Q_n)$, consisting of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most one, i.e., linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. An interpolation projector $P$ is introduced that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, using nodes within $Q_n$. When the number of nodes is an Hadamard number, a non-degenerate simplex can be formed with vertices at $Q_n$. Various methods will be discussed for establishing upper bounds for the norm of $P$ in the form $\|P\|_{Q_n} \leq c \sqrt{n}$ for the corresponding interpolation projector $P$. Special cases of these methods will be applied to specific situations. Next, a number of strategies will be presented to tackle the problem of finding an upper limit for the norm of $P$ when the simplex's diameter is known to be one, in the form $\|P\|_{Q_n} \leq c \sqrt{n}$ for the associated interpolation projector $P$. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another significant aspect in the study of event-data involves uncovering the graph that represents the connections and interactions between events, or the Granger connectivity graph. We have established the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating this graph, particularly showing that the posterior distribution converges to the correct adjacency matrix, as does a Bayesian estimator based on a suitable loss function. This research was motivated by an analysis of EEG data during which two types of neuronal events, neural activity and brain waves, were recorded, and it demonstrates the effectiveness of the Bayesian approach in identifying the connections and underlying mechanisms underlying this data. This has been further validated by a custom-made simulation program. This study has been published in the journal Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. A related earlier work on the estimation of the Granger connectivity graph using Bayesian methods, particularly a results on the posterior distribution's concentration, has also been published in the journal Neural Information Processing Systems. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. These simulations took the initial state of a rotating star, then over time stepped through the Euler and Einstein equations to update the properties of each fluid element, ultimately yielding a wide range of outcomes, from gradual cooling to mass loss and mass accretion, all marked by an exceptionally small computational footprint. 

One such simulation even accurately modeled the collapse of a rotating star under its own gravity, ultimately transforming into a rotating protneutron star, from which we derived valuable insights about this complex event. This new approach offers a powerful and versatile tool for studying the evolution of rotating stars, and our results show that this method is capable of handling a wide range of problems, from simple to highly complex scenarios, all with a relatively minimal computational requirement. 

This approach is now available as the RANSOME code, awaiting public access on the website of the Astrophysical Simulation Consortium.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. We highlight the network's potential applications, including the incorporation of additional features that could further enhance its performance. Furthermore, the trained model's recovery of neutron star and binary neutron star events in real LIGO data holds value in itself. We outline possible paths for improving the network, including exploring alternative deep learning methods and analyzing the dense matter properties of neutron stars.
