We examine its performance, discuss its limitations, and outline possible paths for improvement. The code for this project is also available on GitHub at https://github.com/DeepLearningGW/DCGC_NSBH.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era. Additionally, this study provides concrete metrics to measure urban diversity, facility usage, and visitation behavior, which can be valuable to researchers, policymakers, and businesses. Lastly, with its focus on concrete quantitative analysis, this study can serve as a template for similar future investigations into other phenomena affecting daily public activities.

Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects. The accretion of these objects by the stellar body could explain the recently observed episodes of rapid growth. By post-processing a prior simulation using a one-dimensional model, researchers found that material accumulating at the inner disk does not always result in significant accretion bursts on its own. Rather, only the impact of high-density objects crossing a critical boundary can produce the observed effects. Key factors affecting accretion bursts include: the behavior of turbulent discs where objects can get stuck, as well as discs powered by magnetic winds that allow for bursts akin to those observed. Furthermore, interactions with thermal instabilities in the inner disk can influence the duration and intensity of bursts, while dense stars or migrating objects can produce different effects, such as mergers rather than bursts, and object disruptions that could result in super-Eddington outflows affecting their surroundings. Finally, in models representing young stellar objects formed through the merger of two stars, researchers found that the outcomes can vary, from the formation of massive stars with close binary companions, to the expulsion of massive objects that could then accrete the remaining mass, resulting in a massive star formed through merger. These possible outcomes have significant implications for the formation and death of massive stars, as well as the environment surrounding them. Lastly, in a related finding, researchers discovered that dense stars can break apart under their own gravity, only to reassemble into a massive star formed through merger, with characteristics similar to those obtained through the direct merger of two stars. The simulations discussed here were conducted as part of the Turbulent Molecular Astrophysics project, a collaborative effort between researchers from Macquarie University, the University of New South Wales, the Australian National University, and the University of Melbourne. The outcomes of these simulations have important implications for understanding the formation and death of massive stars, as well as the surrounding environment, and highlight the critical role that accretion and mergers play in shaping these outcomes. The simulations also demonstrate the value of observing protostars at a molecular level, as well as the necessity of employing three-dimensional simulations that take into account the influence of magnetic winds, turbulent motion, and thermal instabilities in the inner disk. The simulations discussed here have been successfully applied to a prior simulation, and as such, represent a significant achievement in post-processing large simulations, as well as a valuable tool for interpreting observational data, particularly in relation to the accretion bursts observed recently. This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We sought to analyze how a uniform shear flow affects weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques. By applying these methods, we obtained a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation describing the time-dependent evolution of the wave envelope. Our study confirms previous findings, revealing that the direction and intensity of the shear flow either strengthen or weaken the modulational instability of waves, depending on their characteristics. Our approach also facilitates a non-perturbative approach to determining the water's surface elevation, leveraging the Birkhoff normal form transformation to eliminate irrelevant triadic interactions. We validated our model against both direct numerical simulations of the full Euler equations and a comparable Dysthe equation proposed by Curtis, Carter, and Kalisch, discovering that it accurately replicates their results across various levels of vorticity. Our research was featured in the Journal of Fluid Mechanics.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in the presence of moving objects. Further testing on a mobile robot in a large open-plan office with real-time 3D navigation using one to five sonar sensors has also been conducted. Extremely compact sonar sensors were used in this test, with real-time 3D navigation demonstrated in a crowded and dynamic environment. The system's modular design allows for easy interchange of sonar sensors, enabling effortless adaptation to varying indoor environments. The navigation system's proficiency was notable, with the robot successfully navigating to designated targets in complex office settings with minimal obstruction. The developed controller and acoustic flow model provide a comprehensive understanding of the system's inner workings, facilitating easy modification and enhancement for future applications. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance. The code is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/abhishek191/TextSum-FakeNews.

A specific application of rotationally invariant L1-PCA to anomaly detection showed promising results and reflected the methodology's potential in such contexts. Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels. When applied to EMO20Q, this approach yields a revised annotation set, alongside a dataset comprising incorrectly annotated instances that can be utilized for future machine learning model training. We also explore the implications of our method for other annotation tasks and discuss its potential applications. The data sets in question, EMO20Q and the BERT-Assisted Annotation Toolkit (BAAT), are available for public use.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  We openly provide the DynaSOAr framework under an permissive BSD license to facilitate easy adoption across a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures.  Our benchmark suite, consisting of both SMMO and non-SMMO applications, is also available for easy testing and comparison purposes.  In particular, DynaSOAr can be used to show that, in many cases, object-oriented programming is just a minor adjustment away from becoming compatible with SIMD devices.  Our research highlights a particular challenge in memory allocation that needs to be addressed in order to support object-oriented programming on SIMD devices, including in particular GPUs.  In response, we created a specific challenge in memory allocation, referred to as the "false sharing" problem, as well as a corresponding efficient solution, called "segregated coalesced memory allocation".  This solution, which is lock-free and parallel, is also efficient in managing both memory usage and memory fragmentation.  We openly provide the source code for both DynaSOAr and our benchmark suite under easy-to-use licenses to facilitate easy adoption and testing purposes. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Lastly, calculations highlight the significance of accurately modeling TiO2's lattice structure, as a perfect cubic structure fails to replicate the experimental results.  Additionally, we investigated various p-atom doped TiO2 stacks and found that both carbon and nitrogen can induce both magnetic and non-magnetic transitions within the material.  Moreover, as the distance between atoms within the stack varies, calculations show that both carbon and nitrogen can induce both magnetic and non-magnetic transitions within the material, including transitions between insulating and metallic states.  We propose that tuning TiO2 stacks by introducing such defects could also enhance its superconducting properties.  Lastly, we investigated N doped TiO2 using VASP with the GI-DFTD method, and found that this approach also accurately replicates the experimental results.  Moreover, as the distance between atoms within the stack varies, calculations show that N doped TiO2 can induce both magnetic and non-magnetic transitions within the material, including transitions between insulating and metallic states.  We propose that tuning TiO2 stacks by introducing such defects could also enhance its superconducting properties.  Lastly, we investigated N doped TiO2 using VASP with the GI-DFTD method, and found that this approach also accurately replicates the experimental results.

Additionally, I discuss the possibilities of discovering the rare decays $t\rightarrow u Z$ and $t\rightarrow c Z$ which could occur at rates too small for detection without employing additional protons tags. In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5. Additionally, we outline an alternative approach to proving upper density estimates, utilizing a concept we call "density operators". Lastly, we pose related questions for future Ramsey theory investigation.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits. Additionally, our study identifies the optimal qudit dimension that minimizes noise tolerance, which is likely situated at the edge of the semi-classical qudit group, possibly including qutrits. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. The temperature sensor was further evaluated in a real-world application, involving the thermal monitoring of a complex 16-bit $\Delta-\Sigma$ ADC chip. The proposed design has a significant impact on the community, with performance characteristics placing it among the top temperature sensors ranked by resolution, inaccuracy, supply voltage range, and static power consumption. The code for this research has been made publicly available on GitHub. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  It is also crucial to investigate the timescales involved in core growth and its potential relation to other factors influencing the outcome of the gravitational collapse, including the level of density and the presence of magnetic fields.  Finally, we discuss the prevalence of core growth in Dragon and the possibility of finding analogous cores in other molecular clouds.  The core growth hypothesis has notable predictions, including the presence of growing cores that are neither protostellar nor starless, and may be identifiable through proper motion studies of related SFRs, and the presence of massive dense core candidates with low internal pressure.  High dynamic range observations of proper motions and associated star formation regions, as well as the analysis of core growth models, are needed to fully explore the core growth hypothesis. Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. The resulting operator leads to the development of the desired positive definite addition formula for spherical random fields. The proposed method's utility is illustrated by establishing the positive definite property of the Kiehl-Pauli differential operator, whose application enables the generation of novel addition formulas for spherical polynomials and allows for a dimension increase of one. The proposed framework also facilitates the exploration of non-uniformly weighted spaces, encompassing the case of Riesz spaces with variable smoothness. The paper also presents a more advanced recurrence that can be utilized to prove the positive definiteness of a class of analytic zonal functions, which includes previously undiscovered cases. The results presented here originate from the author's works on this topic, specifically the papers titled "Positive definite operators and recurrent relations for zonal functions on the sphere" and "The Kiehl-Pauli operator and its applications in spherical context". The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. This relationship offers a practical explanation for the exclusive appearance of the stick-slip or stationary regimes within specific roughness intervals. The effectiveness of our "leverage rule" and the "roughness factor" is illustrated by demonstrating how they account for changes in stress patterns when the mobility of foams is altered, in response to changes in surface roughness, area reduction, or the presence of surfactants. The development of these rules provides a practical tool for predicting the exclusive appearance of the stick-slip or stationary regimes within certain roughness intervals, offering further insight into the unique behavior of dry liquid foams. The unique behavior of dry liquid foams under surface roughness conditions may also be relevant to other complex systems of moving solid or fluid surfaces. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. The code and model used in this report are available online.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/ghrua/look-ahead-attention.

Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. Overall, our goal is to contribute a specific and general knowledge to the field of translational computer science. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. Furthermore, it was discovered that a specific feature of the plasma, a double-shoulder distribution of electron density, is a hallmark of helicon mode, which was validated through simulation. IShTAR's plasma source has been refined to provide both helicon mode and variable wave absorption, making it a valuable tool for studying ICRF wave interaction with plasma. It is now being upgraded to include a longer plasma source, and will contribute to the development of new, more efficient ICRF antennas for the next-generation of fusion devices.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Moreover, this way of dividing the task enables researchers to train separate models for different pathology images, facilitating the reuse of these models. Experimentation with multiple datasets reveals that the W-Shaped Network consistently outperforms standard U-Net based models in terms of evaluation metrics. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/zhkscodeworkgroup/W-Net.

Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. Furthermore, our algorithm yields an approximation factor of $O(\Delta^{1/4})$ in its final output, achieving the same level of performance as existing one-pass algorithms while surpassing the storage limitations of those methods. When the data distribution is uniformly distributed according to the Gaussian distribution with an isotropic covariance matrix, we derive an exact storage capacity without any dimension-dependent storage, resulting in the first algorithm for this specific distribution to achieve both linear dependence on $k$ and a specific error bound without any dependence on $\Delta$. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Moreover, by incorporating inter-grid dynamics, our model can tackle more complex scenarios. Code is available at: https://github.com/kaust-HCI/hierarchical-pursuit_evasion.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our results demonstrate that model-based multi-task reinforcement
learning can also excel at exploiting task synergies when employing modular
dynamics models. Moreover, our work is accompanied by resource-conscious
methodologies, such as employing compact models and a new threshold-based
episode termination policy. Finally, our study yields a related theoretical
analysis, with both a lower bound for shared dynamics models and an upper bound
for isolated networks, providing valuable insights into the relationship between
performance and model size. Along with affirmative results, we also present a
more challenging Vizdoom scenario, showing that even though there is a gap
between the learner's ability and the ease of solving the task with small
isolated networks, the former is still within the realm of possibility. Along
with code available at https://github.com/ghaleem/MMDM-Baseline.

By integrating these theorems, we establish a unified context highlighting their distinct variations' obtainment. Furthermore, this integration becomes the foundation for demonstrating the undecidability of first-order arithmetic and harnesses the Diagonal Lemma's applications, including an undiamondability theorem. Given the ill-posed nature of these problems, researchers rely on regularized optimization techniques to achieve the restoration. Unlike direct optimization approaches, we propose a method that uses Conditional GANs to sample from the posterior distribution of the original data. This results in a non-trivial minimization problem for the network, allowing us to draw on the principles of regularized optimization. The proposed framework, a regularized Conditional GAN, is tested on image deblurring, image compression, and image super-resolution cases. This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. Throughout this discussion, we emphasize the crucial role that symmetry plays in dynamical systems and the limited applicability of fractional-order systems to model certain phenomena due to the absence of smooth, invariant manifolds that are characteristic of other dynamical systems. Lastly, we provide a brief overview of some open research questions related to fractional-order systems. The article presented at the 2022 IEEE Conference on Control and Automation (ICCFA) held in Toronto, Canada.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This finding is supported by similar results from previous studies of the same screens based on polarization measurements. Furthermore, it was discovered that the void's dimensions can be characterized as a spherical bubble with a diameter of approximately 8.37 parsecs, although more precise determination of its shape is needed. The analysis of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit also revealed the orientation of the screen's major axis, which coincides with the galactic plane, and its velocity components perpendicular to the line of sight. The analysis of data from different observing periods allowed for validation of the model of screen invariance over time, with any detected changes occurring on a timescale of a few decades. The spaces inhabited by the screens and the pulsar are likely subject to dynamic variations in the surrounding interstellar medium, which can be studied further with additional observations. The approach used in this study can be applied to other pulsars with similar scintillation patterns, although they likely have longer pulse periods which would require longer observing periods to complete a full orbit. The insights gained from this study about the Local Bubble's morphology are significant, given its proximity to the Solar System and the emptying timescales of this bubble. The analysis of the screen's velocity components perpendicular to the line of sight, in addition to the orientation of the screen's major axis, also provides new insights into the dynamics of the Local Bubble's formation. The discovery of the void within the Local Bubble is significant, as it is likely associated with the spaces inhabited by the screens and the pulsar, specifically within the Gouda cloud. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Code for Quasi-Periodic WaveNet is available at: https://github.com/Esrar/QPNet.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our network's difficulty-aware design provides valuable insights for researchers by offering a clear understanding of how sound source localization works and can be improved. Our code along with the VGG-Sound Source dataset are available for public use.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry.
